features.name: Portable machines
features.what: Small, light machines with a case, for travel and the home.

features.name: Ink ribbon
features.what: An inked fabric ribbon between the type and the paper, in place of ink pads and rollers.
features.today: Typewriters to the end; impact and receipt printers still use ribbons.

features.name: Space bar
features.what: One long bar under the keys that moves the carriage one space without printing.

features.name: QWERTY keyboard
features.what: The Sholes and Glidden layout, which Remington's success made the norm; rivals such as the Ideal (DHIATENSOR) layout lost out.
features.today: Still the standard layout of computer and phone keyboards.

features.name: Shift key (case shift)
features.what: Two characters on each type bar or row, and a key that shifts the carriage or the type basket so the second one prints: half the keys for the same character set.

features.name: Line-end bell
features.what: A bell that rings a few characters before the right margin.

features.name: Interchangeable type
features.what: A type wheel, shuttle or sleeve that lifts out, so one machine writes in several typefaces or languages.
features.today: Changeable fonts: the Selectric's golf ball (1961), daisy wheels, then digital fonts.

features.name: Proportional spacing
features.what: Each letter takes a space to suit its width (m wide, i narrow) instead of one fixed pitch; IBM's Executive (1944) brought it to offices.
features.today: Proportional fonts: nearly all text today.

features.name: Correction and erasing
features.what: Ways to remove or cover a mistake: erasing tables and shields, then (after 1950) correcting ribbons.

features.name: Automatic ribbon reverse
features.what: The ribbon spools change direction by themselves when one runs empty.

features.name: Carriage return and line space
features.what: One lever that turns the platen to the next line and pushes the carriage back to the start.
features.today: The Return or Enter key; CR and LF in character codes (ASCII, 1963).

features.name: Margin stops and release
features.what: Adjustable stops for the left and right margins, and a key to type past them.

features.name: Electric drive
features.what: A motor or magnets do the work of the type stroke and carriage, so a light touch prints evenly.
features.today: Electric and electronic typewriters, then computer keyboards.

features.name: Visible writing
features.what: Type that strikes the front of the platen, so the typist sees the line as it is written; on early understrike machines the writing was hidden until the carriage was lifted.
features.today: Seeing the text as you type, on every later typewriter and every screen.

features.name: Tabulator
features.what: Stops set along the carriage and a key that runs the carriage to the next one, for columns and indents.
features.today: The Tab key and tab stops (HT in ASCII).

features.name: Shift lock
features.what: Holds the shift down for a run of capitals.

features.name: Decimal tabulator
features.what: A row of tab keys for units, tens, hundreds and so on, so figures line up on the decimal point.
features.today: Decimal tab stops in word processors.

features.name: Backspace
features.what: A key that moves the carriage back one space, to correct or to overstrike.

features.name: Two-colour ribbon
features.what: A ribbon with two bands (usually black and red) and a lever that lifts the ribbon to print in the second colour.

landmarks.claim: A second patent of 14 July 1868 covers the earlier wire-linked version of the Milwaukee machine.

landmarks.event: Sholes, Glidden & Soule patent the type-writer
landmarks.claim: Sholes, Glidden and Soule of Milwaukee receive US patent 79,265 for "Improvement in type-writing machines", the patent from which the name "type-writer" spread.

landmarks.event: Remington contracts to build the Sholes & Glidden
landmarks.claim: On 1 March 1873 Densmore signs with E. Remington & Sons, whose mechanics Jenne and Clough rework the Milwaukee machine for mass production (at least 1,000 machines).

landmarks.event: Carriage return by foot treadle, soon replaced by a hand lever
landmarks.claim: The Sholes & Glidden returns its carriage with a foot treadle on its sewing-machine stand; it was quickly displaced by a hand lever.

landmarks.event: Sholes & Glidden goes on sale with the QWERTY keyboard
landmarks.claim: The Sholes & Glidden reaches the market on 1 July 1874 with four rows of keys in the QWERTY order, typing capitals only, as a blind (understrike) writer at about $125.

landmarks.event: Sholes & Glidden prints through a travelling inked ribbon
landmarks.claim: The first production typewriter prints through an inked ribbon that travels across the printing point with the carriage, the arrangement every later standard machine kept.

landmarks.event: Bell warns of the line end
landmarks.claim: On the early Remington shift-key machines a bell rings several spaces before the end of the writing line.

landmarks.event: Remington No. 2 adds the shift key
landmarks.claim: Remington No. 2 adds a shift key, so one key types both a capital and a small letter; Brooks's 1878 patent shifts the platen between two types on each bar.
Sholes's patent of 27 August 1878 is the first documented appearance of the QWERTY layout in a patent.
James B. Hammond patents a type-wheel machine whose type shuttle can be swapped in seconds to change typeface or language; the Hammond No. 1 reached buyers in 1884.

landmarks.machine: Caligraph No. 1 (caps only) and Caligraph No. 2 (upper and lower case)
landmarks.claim: The Caligraph gives every character its own key (a double keyboard) instead of a shift, the first such commercial typebar machine.
Crandall's type sleeve, a removable cylinder carrying all the characters, goes into production with the Crandall No. 1 in 1883 after his 1881 patent.

landmarks.event: Yost: ink pad instead of a ribbon
landmarks.claim: The Yost drops the ribbon: its typebars rest on a ring-shaped felt ink pad and print directly, through a type guide that keeps alignment.

landmarks.event: Columbia Bar-Lock: early downstrike visible writer
landmarks.claim: The Bar-Lock's typebars strike down onto the top of the platen, so the typist can see the line, and it was claimed as the first keyed visible writer on the market.
Josiah B. Gathright patents a tabulating stop that jumps the carriage to set columns, later held by a US appeals court to be the first commercially successful tabulator.
Lyman C. Smith markets Alexander T. Brown's Smith Premier, which became the leading double-keyboard machine and had a built-in type-cleaning brush.
James D. Daugherty patents a front-strike typebar machine; the Daugherty Visible was among the first to type in full view with a four-bank keyboard and single shift.
The Densmore, launched in 1891 with ball-bearing typebars, is credited with introducing the back-spacer "in a practical manner".
Thomas Oliver patents his U-shaped downstrike typebars; the Oliver went on sale around 1894-95 and became the most successful downstrike visible writer.
Blickensderfer's light type-wheel machine, patented in 1892 and shown at the 1893 Chicago World's Fair, is the first portable produced in quantity, with an interchangeable type wheel.
A later Crandall model carries a ribbon mechanism for two colours, one of the earliest two-colour ribbons on an American machine.

landmarks.event: Union Typewriter Co. makes QWERTY the standard
landmarks.claim: Five large US makers merge as the Union Typewriter Company in 1893 and adopt QWERTY, after which it is the industry standard.

landmarks.event: Wagner visible-writing patent (basis of the Underwood)
landmarks.claim: The front-strike visible-writing patent behind the Underwood is issued on 31 July 1894, filed by Herman L. Wagner and assigned to his father Franz X. Wagner.
The Bar-Lock No. 4 carries a tabulator under Spiro patents of 23 July 1895, claimed by the trade press as the first practical tabulator.
Remington fits the first automatic ribbon reverse, by George B. Webb, so typists no longer had to reverse the ribbon by hand.
The Underwood No. 1 strikes the front of the platen so the whole line stays in view, the layout that every standard typewriter later copied.

landmarks.event: Underwood builds the tabulator into the machine
landmarks.claim: The Underwood is the first machine with a tabulator built in at no extra charge, for setting work in neat columns.

landmarks.event: Gorin decimal tabulator on the Remington
landmarks.claim: The Gorin Tabulator, the first decimal tabulator, appears as a Remington attachment and steps the carriage to units, tens or hundreds for columns of figures.
Hammond offers a back-spacing attachment, standard on new machines from 1 December 1898, one of the earliest backspace keys.
Thaddeus Cahill patents and builds an electric typewriter, called the first electric typewriter made in series.
The Underwood No. 5 (front-strike, four-bank, single shift, visible) begins production in 1900 and sets the standard form of the office typewriter for decades.
Blickensderfer builds a motor-driven type-wheel typewriter, an early electric that failed commercially because electric supply was not standardised.
Frank Rose's folding typebar portable, whose platen folds over the keyboard, is the ancestor of the Corona.
The Remington No. 10 of 1908 is the first visible typewriter sold under the Remington name, marking the end of the blind-writer era among the big makers.
By 1909 the two-colour (bichrome) ribbon with a colour selector is almost universal on standard machines; Underwood adds it to the No. 5 around 1908-09.

landmarks.event: Built-in tabulator and backspace become standard
landmarks.claim: By 1909 every "standard" machine has a built-in tabulator at no extra cost and the back-space key is found even on low-priced machines.
Kidder's Noiseless replaces the hammer blow with a pressing typebar so the machine is quiet; a cam-driven first model was replaced by Anderson's 1912 type action.
Remington brings out the first key-set decimal tabulator, letting the operator set column stops from the keyboard.
The three-bank, folding Corona No. 3 becomes the first typebar portable to sell widely.
James Fields Smathers files in 1912 for a power-driven typewriter that needs less effort to operate; his design later underlay the Remington Electric and the Electromatic.
The Remington Portable is the first portable with the full four-row standard keyboard, shown at the New York Business Show in October 1920.
Remington sells an electric typewriter built on its No. 12 with Northeast Electric motors and Smathers's design; about 2,500 were made.
Northeast Electric produces its own Electromatic electric typewriter after the Remington deal lapses.
IBM, having bought Electromatic in 1933, issues the improved Electric Model 01, the first commercially successful electric typewriter in the US.
The IBM Executive gives each letter a width in units of 1/32 inch (proportional spacing), so typed pages look typeset; announced 1941 but delayed by the war until 1944.
